subject.title: May
subject.author: Seamus Heaney
subject.text:
When I looked down from the bridge
Trout were flipping the sky
Into smithereens, the stones
Of the wall warmed me.

Wading green stems, lugs of leaf
That untangle and bruise
(Their tiny gushers of juice)
My toecaps sparkle now

Over the soft fontanel
Of Ireland. I should wear
Hide shoes, the hair next my skin,
For walking this ground:


Wasn't there a spa-well,
Its coping grassy, pendent?
And then the spring issuing
Right across the tarmac.

I'm out to find that village,
Its low sills fragrant
With lady's-smock and celandine,
Marshlights in the summer dark.

title: A Word for Bomb Damage, Spent on a Fish
standfirst: Seamus Heaney wrote this small, five-stanza walk through his home ground while the book it belongs to was still called Winter Seeds — and revised it, over the following six months, into something that could survive internment and Bloody Sunday intact. The gentlest word in the poem turns out to be the one that couldn't stay innocent.

sections.heading: A Fish Breaks the Sky Into a Word for Bomb Damage
sections.body:
Nothing large happens in "May." A man on a bridge watches a trout rise: "When I looked down from the bridge / Trout were flipping the sky / Into smithereens, the stones / Of the wall warmed me." Five unrhymed quatrains follow, most lines running to five or six syllables, and the poem never again reaches for anything bigger than that first small collision of fish and reflection.

The word doing the damage has a history worth pausing on. Smithereens comes from the Irish smidirín, the diminutive of smiodar, a broken piece — the same -een ending that gives English colleen and poteen. Its first recorded English use, in 1795, was a notice posted in County Wexford in which Orangemen threatened to "break your carriage in smithereens"; from there the word spread through Irish, British and American newspapers until, by the twentieth century, it had settled almost entirely into two stock phrases — [blown to smithereens](https://www.worldwidewords.org/qa-smi1.html) and smashed to smithereens. It is, in other words, a word for total, violent fragmentation, on loan here to describe a fish disturbing a river.

Heaney was finishing the book this poem belongs to in the eighteen months either side of that word's usual modern meaning becoming impossible to hold at arm's length. He uses it anyway, for a trout.

sections.heading: The Bridge He Had Been Walking to Since He Was a Boy
sections.body:
The bridge in the first line is not generic. Heaney was born on Mossbawn, his family's farm in the townland of Tamniarn near Castledawson, Co. Derry, and its fields ran down to the [River Moyola](https://www.writeoutloud.net/public/blogentry.php?blogentryid=118240), half a mile from the front door. As a boy he walked that river to the stone arches of the railway bridge at Castledawson — the same stretch of water he returns to elsewhere in this collection, in "A New Song."

That matters for how much weight the poem's small, deliberately unnamed details can carry. "That village," the spa-well, the low sills fragrant with lady's-smock and celandine — none of it is invented scenery. It is a specific, half-mile-square piece of South Derry that Heaney had known on foot since childhood, described in a book whose other poems name it outright: Broagh, Anahorish, Toome. "May" is the one that doesn't put a name to the place, which is part of what makes the poem feel like a private errand rather than a public statement — a walk taken for its own sake, back to ground the poet already owned by heart.

sections.heading: The Soft Unfused Part of a Country
sections.body:
The poem's second image is stranger than its first. Wading through spring undergrowth, the speaker finds his "toecaps sparkle now / Over the soft fontanel / Of Ireland." A fontanel is the unfused gap in an infant skull, where the bone hasn't yet closed over the brain — Heaney is describing solid ground as though it were an exposed, unhealed part of a body, still soft enough to be hurt.

It is not a one-off figure. The same book's best-known poem, "The Tollund Man," turns an Iron Age body pulled intact from a Jutland peat bog into a way of thinking about Irish violence and preservation — and the collection's own working title, before Heaney changed it, was Winter Seeds, a phrase lifted directly from that poem, for the grain found undigested in the dead man's stomach. Land-as-body and body-preserved-in-land are the same habit of mind running through the whole collection; "May" applies it in miniature, to a country instead of a corpse, and to a walk instead of a two-thousand-year-old exhumation.

sections.heading: From Watching to Walking
sections.body:
The poem's real engine is a change of mood, stanza by stanza, from passive to active. It opens with the speaker doing nothing but looking; even the warmth he feels comes from the bridge's stones, not from him. The close reader Nigel Assam, writing on the poem, calls the trout's disturbance "an elegant description, just enough of explosion included" — precise, and still contained.

The turn comes mid-poem, in a single modal verb: "I should wear / Hide shoes, the hair next my skin." Should is a decision taking shape, not yet a decision made — and Heaney places it, tellingly, straddling a line break, the poem's white space acting as the gap in which the thought actually forms. Two stanzas later the hedging is gone entirely: "I'm out to find that village." No modal verb qualifies it. What began as a man glancing over a wall ends as a man in motion, committed to a specific destination, and the whole poem is the four short steps between those two states.

The last line refuses to resolve as neatly as the plot does. "Marshlights in the summer dark" pairs a season of long evenings with the dark it should not yet have — a small contradiction Heaney lets stand, rather than tidying away, on the poem's final beat.

sections.heading: A Manuscript Called Winter Seeds
sections.body:
"May" was written, along with the rest of this collection, between 1969 and 1971 — much of it while Heaney was a visiting lecturer at Berkeley in 1970–71, before he came back to a Belfast that was, in the blogger and critic Sheila O'Malley's phrase, about to have "everything explode." He returned to his lectureship at Queen's University Belfast in the autumn of 1971 with a manuscript already assembled, and its title at that point was Winter Seeds — a safe, rural phrase, borrowed from "The Tollund Man," that told a browsing reader nothing at all.

He did not send that version to Faber. Between his return to Belfast and the typescript he actually dispatched — dated 14 October 1971 — and the six months of further revision that followed before publication, he retitled the book Wintering Out and expanded it from seventy-two poems to eighty. Wintering out is a phrase farmers use for livestock that survive a hard winter without shelter; as a title for a book being finished while Northern Ireland came apart, it stopped being a pastoral word and became a fairly exact description of what the book, and its author, were trying to do.

sections.heading: The Six Months the Country Didn't Give Him
sections.body:
Line up the dates and the pastoral reading of "May" gets harder to hold onto without qualification. Internment without trial began in Northern Ireland on 9 August 1971 — Operation Demetrius, more than three hundred people arrested overnight, twenty-four deaths in the rioting that followed within days — a matter of weeks before Heaney came back from California to a Belfast lectureship he still held. Bloody Sunday followed on 30 January 1972, when British paratroopers shot twenty-six unarmed civilians during a march against internment in Derry, killing fourteen; it fell squarely inside the six months in which Heaney was still reworking the manuscript he had already renamed once.

Wintering Out reached print that November. Reviewers at the time were divided over how directly it engaged with any of this — some read its politics as newly serious, others were disappointed it did not confront the violence more explicitly — but the book they were arguing about had itself been rewritten, mid-composition, by the same events. "May" sits inside that rewritten book: a poem about a walk toward a hidden village, finished in the same stretch of months in which the country the walk is set in was busy becoming a different, harder subject.

sections.heading: The Walk He Took With His Whole Life a Few Months Later
sections.body:
In 1972, not long after Wintering Out went to press, Heaney resigned his lectureship at Queen's and moved his family to a cottage in Glanmore, Co. Wicklow, in the Republic — out of the North entirely, to write full-time. He always rejected the suggestion that he had fled the Troubles, but the move read, to some critics and to some of his own countrymen, as exactly that: a poet with a rooted claim on this landscape choosing to watch it from across a border. Three years later, in "Exposure," the last poem of North, he gave the accusation a name of his own choosing: "I am neither internee nor informer: / An inner emigre grown long-haired / And thoughtful."

The critic Michael Schmidt's rebuttal to that self-charge is the sharper way to read it back into "May": the Troubles, he argues, "are not external to one whose community is riven by them, nor do they become external when he leaves." Read that way, this poem's small, determined walk toward a half-remembered village — the modal hedging burned off, the destination named, nothing waiting to stop him — looks less like an escape from politics than a rehearsal for the literal one Heaney made with his own life within the year: leaving is not the same as no longer being implicated, and the walker who finally says "I'm out to find that village" was, in a sense, already practising the sentence he would shortly have to mean.
